categories: [biomechanics, gait, cross-modal, canonical-correlation, validated]

> **What this case shows** — three cross-modal questions, one data set. Having asked
> whether gait kinematics and kinetics are *dependent at all* (distance correlation)
> and whether they share a *representational geometry* (RSA), the natural third
> question is the classical one: what is the maximal **linear** relationship between
> them? **Canonical correlation analysis** (Hotelling 1936) answers it by finding the
> weighted combination of knee+ankle angles and the weighted combination of ground
> forces that correlate most strongly. On real WBDS walking that first canonical
> correlation is **0.737** (second 0.299), strong and consistent across five subjects
> (0.74–0.85). The ecosystem's `cca` reproduces base R's **`stats::cancor`** — a
> non-trivial, independent SVD computation — to **machine precision** (max |diff| =
> 1.1×10⁻¹⁶). And tellingly, that 0.737 is almost the distance correlation on the same
> data (0.72): the coupling is **largely linear**, captured by a single canonical pair.

::: {.callout-tip title="The recipe you'll learn"}
**Workflow** — for two aligned blocks: call `cca(X, Y)` → read the **canonical
correlations** (`$cor`) and, if you need them, the canonical coefficients/scores.
**Way of thinking** — CCA is the *linear* cross-modal lens: it asks for the best
linear combination of each block. Reading its first canonical correlation *next to* a
nonlinear dependence measure (distance correlation) tells you how much of the coupling
is linear — if they agree, a single linear pair explains it.
**Ecosystem usage** — `PhysioCrossModal::cca()`, alongside `distanceCorrelation()`
(any dependence), `representationalSimilarity()` (rank geometry), `jive()` and
`multipleFactorAnalysis()` for the rest of the cross-modal toolkit.
:::

## Proposition

On real WBDS walking, the first canonical correlation between gait kinematics and
kinetics is 0.737 (WBDS01) and 0.74–0.85 (mean 0.79) across five subjects, and `cca`
reproduces base R's `stats::cancor` to machine precision (max |diff| = 1.1×10⁻¹⁶).

## Question & goal

**The question is the maximal linear coupling between two modalities — and whether the
ecosystem computes it exactly.** Canonical correlation is a non-trivial eigenvalue/SVD
problem, so a correct implementation must match the reference. The goal is a
head-to-head against base R's `stats::cancor`, and a comparison of the first canonical
correlation to the distance correlation to see how *linear* the coupling is.

## Challenge & approach

The two blocks live in different units, so we ask CCA for the linear combinations that
line up best. We compute the canonical correlations with `cca` and with `stats::cancor`
and compare — expecting an exact match — then read the first canonical correlation
beside the distance correlation.

```
knee+ankle angles ┐
                  ├─ cca → canonical correlations (r1, r2)   (== stats::cancor)
AP+vertical GRF   ┘         r1 vs distance correlation → how linear?
```

## Data

**WBDS — Fukuchi, Fukuchi & Duarte (2018), PeerJ** (figshare 5722711, CC-BY 4.0): five
subjects of treadmill walking. Sagittal **knee + ankle flexion angles** and the
**antero-posterior + vertical GRF**, 450 aligned samples — the *same* blocks as the
[dCor](../crossmodal-dcor-gait-wbds/) and [RSA](../rsa-mantel-gait-wbds/) cases. Details
in [`artifacts/data_sources.json`](artifacts/data_sources.json).

## Results

![Left: the first canonical variate pair for WBDS01 — the kinematic canonical variate against the kinetic one; CCA rotates each block so this pair correlates as strongly as possible (r1 = 0.737, exactly stats::cancor). Right: the first canonical correlation for all five subjects (0.74–0.85, mean 0.79) — a strong, consistent linear coupling.](artifacts/figure.png)

*How to read this:* CCA finds the single best linear "view" of each block; the left
panel is those two views plotted against each other, and their correlation is r1.

| Quantity | This reproduction | Reference |
|---|---|---|
| First canonical correlation r1 | **0.7371** | `stats::cancor` = 0.7371 |
| Second canonical correlation r2 | **0.2988** | `stats::cancor` = 0.2988 |
| max \|diff\| vs cancor | **1.1×10⁻¹⁶** | 0 (identical) |
| Mean r1, 5 subjects | **0.7949** | — |
| Distance correlation (same data) | 0.72 | *(dCor case)* |

The op reproduces `stats::cancor` exactly, the coupling is strong across subjects, and
r1 ≈ dCor says it is largely linear. Values trace to
[`artifacts/cca_summary.csv`](artifacts/cca_summary.csv) and
[`artifacts/cca_by_subject.csv`](artifacts/cca_by_subject.csv).

## Conclusion

Canonical correlation gives the linear lens on gait's kinematics–kinetics coupling, and
the ecosystem computes it exactly as base R does. The transferable takeaway: **use CCA
for the maximal linear relationship between two modalities, and read its first canonical
correlation next to a nonlinear dependence measure — when they agree, as here (0.74 vs
0.72), a single linear canonical pair explains the coupling.** Across the three cases —
distance correlation (any dependence, 0.72), RSA (rank geometry, 0.34), CCA (linear
canonical, 0.74) — the same data has been read through three lenses, each validated
against a different canonical reference.

## Open questions

- CCA also yields the canonical **loadings** — which kinematic and kinetic degrees of
  freedom drive the coupling — and higher-dimensional blocks (all joint angles vs the
  full GRF + moments) would reveal more canonical pairs. A **regularized/sparse CCA**
  would handle wide blocks and select the driving variables; comparing loadings across
  subjects or against a clinical group would turn this validated estimator into a
  cross-modal coordination study. The near-equality of r1 and the distance correlation
  also invites a systematic map of *when* a coupling is linear. *Documented, not
  escalated.*

## Using this in your own analysis

| Step | Function | Package |
|---|---|---|
| canonical correlation (linear) | `cca()` | PhysioCrossModal |
| distance correlation (any dependence) | `distanceCorrelation()` | PhysioCrossModal |
| representational similarity (rank geometry) | `representationalSimilarity()` | PhysioCrossModal |
| shared vs individual structure | `jive()` | PhysioCrossModal |

**Choosing the parameters.**

- **Blocks** — pass the two matrices with the same rows (aligned observations); CCA
  finds the best linear combinations, so no channel pre-selection.
- **Number of canonical pairs** — at most `min(ncol(X), ncol(Y))`; here 2. Read them in
  order — r1 is the strongest.
- **Regularization** — for wide/collinear blocks use `lambda_x` / `lambda_y` > 0
  (ridge-regularized CCA) to stabilize the solution.
- **Interpretation** — compare r1 to a nonlinear dependence measure; if r1 ≈ dCor the
  coupling is essentially linear.

**The recipe, copy-runnable:**

```r
library(PhysioCrossModal)

# X = kinematics (n x p), Y = kinetics (n x q), same rows
cc <- cca(X, Y)
cc$cor          # c(0.7371, 0.2988) -- the canonical correlations

# exact by construction: matches base R's stats::cancor
stopifnot(max(abs(cc$cor - stats::cancor(X, Y)$cor)) < 1e-9)
```

**Auditing the numbers.** Every value on this page traces to
